screens.title: Factory Method Pattern: Delegating Object Creation
screens.narratorSegment: In real applications you'll often see classes that directly instantiate other classes with the new keyword. That works at first, but it couples a client to concrete types and forces changes when new product types appear. The Factory Method pattern offers a lighter-weight way to fix that: a Creator declares a factory method that returns a Product, and subclasses override that method to return specific Concrete Products. Practically, your core logic works only with the Product interface and a Creator contract; concrete types are injected by subclassing a Creator. For example, a notification service can accept a NotificationCreator and call its NotifyUser method, never needing to know whether the underlying product is an email, an SMS, or a push message. This makes the system open for extension — you add a new Concrete Product and Concrete Creator — and closed for modification — you do not change the existing Creator or client code. Watch for over-engineering: if you truly never expect more than one product type, the added indirection can be unnecessary. As you explore the lessons ahead, notice the roles Product, Concrete Product, Creator, and Concrete Creator, and think about which classes in your codebase might benefit from delegating object creation.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Delegate object creation with a factory method so clients depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. This reduces coupling and supports extension without modifying existing code.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › Factory Method Overview
Factory Method Pattern
Delegate creation to subclasses so your core logic stays decoupled and extensible.
In this lesson
You will learn the four roles of the Factory Method, see a C# notification example, and practice refactoring a logger to use this pattern.
Why it matters
Reducing direct new calls prevents tight coupling, supports the Open/Closed Principle, and makes future extension safer and easier.
Explore Key Topics
Product Interface
Defines the common contract
Concrete Creators
Return specific products
Open/Closed
Extend without modifying
Concept sketch
Creator delegates — Concrete Creators produce Concrete Products
Product
Interface or abstract class that defines the contract for created objects.
Creator
Declares the factory method and may contain business logic that uses the Product.
Concrete Creator
Overrides the factory method to instantiate a Concrete Product.
Note: This view is a static learning sketch to orient the chapter.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why direct 'new' calls create tight coupling and how the Factory Method pattern resolves that by delegating object creation. You will identify the four roles: Product, Concrete Product, Creator, and Concrete Creator, and describe the responsibilities of each role. You will implement the pattern in C# by defining a Product interface, concrete product classes, an abstract Creator with a factory method, and concrete creators that override it. Finally, you will analyze when the pattern is a good fit and recognize common pitfalls like confusing it with a simple factory or over-engineering when only one product exists. For example, you'll refactor a simple ConsoleLogger into a LoggerCreator and a ConsoleLoggerCreator so the application can accept future file or database loggers without modifying the application class. These competencies prepare you to design extensible code that follows the Open/Closed Principle and reduces maintenance friction in growing systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to understanding the pattern, you will practice refactoring a simple logger scenario and complete assessment questions that test recognition of pattern roles and correct usage. The hands-on activity asks you to define an ILogger interface, make ConsoleLogger implement it, create a LoggerCreator abstract class with an abstract CreateLogger method and a PerformLogging helper, then implement a ConsoleLoggerCreator and update the Application to accept a LoggerCreator. Running the refactored program should still produce the same console output but now allow adding file or database loggers without changing Application. The assessment includes multiple-choice questions that check whether you can distinguish Factory Method from Simple Factory and identify Concrete Creators in code snippets. Practicing the refactor reinforces the advantages: decoupling, easier extension, and adherence to the Open/Closed Principle. Also practice spotting the common mistake: adding a static factory that requires modification for each new product. That contrast sharpens your judgment about when the Factory Method is the right choice.

Refactor ConsoleLogger into Product/Creator so Application accepts a LoggerCreator. This prepares the system for file or database loggers in future without modifying Application.
Starter code (concept)
// ConsoleLogger
public class ConsoleLogger
{
  public void Log(string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"[Console Log] {message}");
  }
}

// Application has direct instantiation
public class Application
{
  private ConsoleLogger _logger;

  public Application()
  {
    _logger = new ConsoleLogger();
  }

  public void Run()
  {
    _logger.Log("Application started.");
    _logger.Log("Application finished.");
  }
}
Assessment
  1. Choose why Factory Method promotes loose coupling.
  2. Identify Concrete Creators in a code snippet.
  3. Explain when the pattern is not worth the cost.

screens.title: Problem: Tight Coupling from direct 'new' calls
screens.narratorSegment: Directly calling new to create objects is common, but it tightly couples the client to concrete classes. That coupling means every time you add a new product variant you may need to change the client code. For example, imagine a reporting module that creates PdfReport, ExcelReport, and CsvReport directly. Adding WordReport forces editing the reporting module, which breaks the Open/Closed Principle. This problem is not just theoretical: tight coupling increases test fragility, makes mocking harder, and centralizes knowledge about concrete types in many places. A common misconception is that using a single central static factory solves the issue. A simple static factory centralizes creation but still requires modification each time a new product type is added; it shifts, rather than eliminates, the place where changes occur. The Factory Method uses inheritance and polymorphism instead. It declares a factory method in a Creator that returns an abstract Product; Concrete Creators override it to return specific Concrete Products. That way, the client depends only on the Creator interface and Product contract and stays unchanged when new variants are introduced. Consider asking: which classes in your codebase currently know about concrete types and would benefit from delegating creation?

keyIdea.title: Problem statement
keyIdea.text: Direct instantiation causes tight coupling. The Factory Method relocates creation responsibility so clients depend only on abstractions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › Tight Coupling Problem
Definition
Tight coupling occurs when a class depends on specific concrete types, preventing extension without modification.
Concrete example
// Reporting module
var report = new PdfReport();
report.Generate();
Adding WordReport would require editing this module — that's the coupling we want to avoid.
Misconception
A Simple Factory centralizes creation using a static method, but it still needs edits when new products are added. The Factory Method uses subclassing so new types can be added by creating new subclasses rather than changing existing code.
Key takeaway
If you foresee multiple product variants or want client code stable, avoid direct new calls and consider a factory method approach.
Check your understanding
List a place in your project where a class uses new. Could that new be deferred to a Creator?
Pro tip
Begin with the Product interface. Define the minimal contract the Creator needs to work with.
Key Takeaway

Avoid direct new calls when future variations are likely; use abstraction to defer creation decisions.

screens.title: Factory Method — The Pattern in Words
screens.narratorSegment: The Factory Method pattern defines a factory method in a Creator, which returns an object typed as Product. The Creator may implement business logic that uses the Product, but it defers the exact instantiation to Concrete Creators. This is different from simply using new: the Creator only relies on the Product contract and the factory method's promise. Concretely, the four roles are Product, Concrete Product, Creator, and Concrete Creator. Product is an interface or abstract class declaring the operations available to clients. Concrete Products implement that interface. Creator is an abstract class or interface that declares an abstract factory method returning a Product; it can also include methods that use the Product. Concrete Creators inherit from Creator and override the factory method to return a specific Concrete Product. A useful mental model is a shop that knows how to process orders but relies on specialized machines to produce items. That separation keeps the shop code stable when new machine types arrive. A common mistake is letting Concrete Products diverge so much that the Product contract no longer supports the Creator's logic; when that happens, the pattern is misapplied and the hierarchy needs redesign.

keyIdea.title: Pattern in brief
keyIdea.text: Provide a factory method in a Creator; let subclasses override it to return different Concrete Products that all follow a shared Product contract.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › Factory Method Definition
Roles and responsibilities
  • Product: contract the client uses.
  • Concrete Product: specific implementation.
  • Creator: declares factory method and uses returned Product.
  • Concrete Creator: overrides factory method to instantiate a Concrete Product.
If Concrete Products diverge too much, the Creator cannot operate polymorphically, signaling a design smell.
Metaphor
Think of a main shop that processes orders and calls a create function. Different machines (subclasses) implement that create function to produce brochures, cards, or banners without changing the shop logic.
Example check
Does your Creator need to know the concrete type? If no, Factory Method may be appropriate.
Common mistake
Confusing Factory Method with Simple Factory; the latter centralizes creation in a static method and must be modified for each new product.
When to avoid
If there is only a single product and no foreseeable need to extend, using the pattern adds unnecessary classes.
Key Takeaway

Factory Method preserves client stability by delegating concrete creation to subclasses that implement a shared Product contract.

screens.title: C# Example — Product and Concrete Products
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at the Product and Concrete Product implementation in C#. The Product is an interface called INotification that declares a Send method. Concrete Products implement that interface: EmailNotification, SmsNotification, and PushNotification. Each one provides the actual sending behavior, but the client will only see the INotification contract. This separation allows code to call Send without caring about transport details. For example, EmailNotification writes a message to the console indicating an email was sent; SmsNotification and PushNotification do similarly for their transports. A common misconception is to design overly broad interfaces that include operations not supported by all concrete types. Keep INotification focused on the minimal contract required by clients that will use it. In the sample code below, each concrete class returns a string acknowledging delivery. That return value shows how concrete implementations may provide behavior-specific details while remaining compatible with the Product interface. As you read the code, think about testability: you can mock INotification in unit tests, isolating client logic from the actual send implementations. C# Example — Product and Concrete Products means design a small, consistent product interface so multiple concrete products can implement it and be used interchangeably by clients.. In practical terms, defining inotification and three concrete implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Product contract
keyIdea.text: Design a small, consistent Product interface so multiple Concrete Products can implement it and be used interchangeably by clients.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › INotification & Implementations
Product: INotification
// Product Interface
public interface INotification
{
  string Send(string recipient, string message);
}
Keep the interface focused: only include what clients require to operate with a notification.
Concrete Products
// EmailNotification
public class EmailNotification : INotification
{
  public string Send(string recipient, string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Sending Email to {recipient}: {message}");
    return $"Email sent to {recipient}.";
  }
}

// SmsNotification
public class SmsNotification : INotification
{
  public string Send(string recipient, string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Sending SMS to {recipient}: {message}");
    return $"SMS sent to {recipient}.";
  }
}

// PushNotification
public class PushNotification : INotification
{
  public string Send(string recipient, string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Sending Push Notification to {recipient}: {message}");
    return $"Push notification sent to {recipient}.";
  }
}
Example
A client can hold an INotification reference and swap concrete implementations for different channels without code changes.
Misconception
Do not bloat the Product interface. If operations differ widely, consider separate product hierarchies.
Key Takeaway

Design concise Product contracts so multiple Concrete Products remain compatible and testable.

screens.title: Creator and Factory Method
screens.narratorSegment: The Creator is an abstract class or interface that declares the factory method returning a Product. It can also contain business logic that uses the returned Product. In our C# example we have an abstract NotificationCreator with an abstract CreateNotification method. NotificationCreator includes a NotifyUser method that calls CreateNotification and then uses INotification. Send to perform work. The key idea is that the Creator defines the workflow while delegating the concrete instantiation to subclasses. This lets the main algorithm remain unchanged while the concrete parts vary. A misconception is thinking the factory method must be public and static. It is typically an instance method you override in subclasses. Another important detail: the Creator may provide default implementations that rely on the factory method, so subclasses need only supply the specific concrete type. Designing Creator methods around the smallest Product contract helps keep the Creator implementation stable as new products are added. Creator and Factory Method means creator declares a factory method and implements business logic that operates on the product returned by that method, enabling polymorphic instantiation.. In practical terms, the creator declares the factory method and uses the product returned. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › NotificationCreator
Creator: NotificationCreator
// Creator Abstract Class
public abstract class NotificationCreator
{
  // The factory method
  public abstract INotification CreateNotification();

  // Other business logic that uses the notification
  public string NotifyUser(string recipient, string message)
  {
    INotification notification = CreateNotification(); // Calls the factory method
    return notification.Send(recipient, message);
  }
}
The CreateNotification method is the extension point subclasses override to change product types.
Design notes
  • Keep CreateNotification focused on returning a Product.
  • Creator can include reusable steps that call the product's methods.
  • Factory method is usually an instance method overridden by subclasses.
Concrete Creator example
EmailNotificationCreator would override CreateNotification to return an EmailNotification.
Misconception
Avoid making the factory method static; subclassing polymorphism is the mechanism that enables extension without modification.
Key Takeaway

Creator defines the algorithm and uses the Product; Concrete Creators supply the specific product types by overriding the factory method.

screens.title: Concrete Creators and Client Usage
screens.narratorSegment: Concrete Creators override the factory method to return concrete products. In our example, classes like EmailNotificationCreator, SmsNotificationCreator, and PushNotificationCreator inherit from NotificationCreator and return the corresponding INotification implementation. The client — for instance a NotificationService — works only with the NotificationCreator contract and calls NotifyUser. It never instantiates concrete notifications directly. This decoupling means adding a new notification type requires only a new Concrete Product and Concrete Creator; the NotificationService code remains unchanged. A concrete example: NotificationService. ProcessNotification accepts a NotificationCreator, recipient, and message, calls creator. NotifyUser, and logs the returned string. One misconception is believing the client must construct the Concrete Creator. In many architectures the Concrete Creator is injected or selected by configuration; the client still works through the Creator interface. This approach improves testability because tests can pass a stub Creator that returns a test double Product, isolating client behavior from concrete sending logic. Concrete Creators and Client Usage means clients operate against creator and product abstractions, so concrete variations can be added without changing client code.. In practical terms, concrete creators return specific products; clients consume the creator interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › Concrete Creators & Client
Concrete Creators
public class EmailNotificationCreator : NotificationCreator
{
  public override INotification CreateNotification()
  {
    return new EmailNotification();
  }
}

public class SmsNotificationCreator : NotificationCreator
{
  public override INotification CreateNotification()
  {
    return new SmsNotification();
  }
}

public class PushNotificationCreator : NotificationCreator
{
  public override INotification CreateNotification()
  {
    return new PushNotification();
  }
}
Client: NotificationService
public class NotificationService
{
  public void ProcessNotification(NotificationCreator creator, string recipient, string message)
  {
    string result = creator.NotifyUser(recipient, message);
    Console.WriteLine($"Service log: {result}");
  }
}
The client passes a Concrete Creator; the service only needs the Creator's interface.
Usage
Call ProcessNotification with different creators to change behavior at runtime without modifying the service.
Testing tip
Inject a test creator that returns a stub notification to isolate and verify client logic.
Key Takeaway

Concrete Creators encapsulate product selection; clients consume creators and remain unaware of concrete product details.

screens.title: Refactor Example: Logger Activity
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on refactor follows a clear sequence. Step one: extract an ILogger interface that declares Log(string message). This is the Product contract. Step two: make the existing ConsoleLogger implement ILogger without changing its behavior. Step three: create an abstract LoggerCreator with an abstract CreateLogger method that returns ILogger, and add a PerformLogging helper that calls CreateLogger and uses Log to write messages. Step four: implement ConsoleLoggerCreator inheriting from LoggerCreator, override CreateLogger to return a new ConsoleLogger. Step five: change Application to accept a LoggerCreator in its constructor and call PerformLogging where it previously used ConsoleLogger directly. Finally, update Program. Main to instantiate Application with ConsoleLoggerCreator. After this change the output remains the same, but adding file or database loggers only requires new Concrete Creator and Concrete Product classes. A common error during refactor is forgetting to change Application's construction site; ensure the constructor signature now receives a LoggerCreator so the dependency is provided externally. This sequence preserves behavior while improving extensibility and testability. Refactor Example: Logger Activity means extract ilogger, implement loggercreator with performlogging, create concrete creator, and inject the creator into application to enable future loggers without modification.. In practical terms, step-by-step refactor from direct instantiation to factory method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Factory Method vs Simple Factory
screens.narratorSegment: It's important to distinguish Factory Method from a Simple Factory. A Simple Factory is a single static function or class that creates objects based on parameters; it centralizes instantiation but still needs to be modified every time a new product type is added. By contrast, the Factory Method leverages subclassing and polymorphism: each Concrete Creator knows how to create its own Concrete Product and new creators can be introduced without changing existing creator code. Use Simple Factory for small programs where centralization simplifies code and changes are rare. Choose Factory Method when you need extensibility, when different modules should provide their own creation logic, or when product creation requires subclass-specific behavior. A common mistake is picking Factory Method for a one-off situation, which increases class count and complexity for no benefit. Conversely, choosing a Simple Factory when extensibility is required will lead to the same maintenance hotspot reappearing wherever the static factory is referenced. The rule of thumb: prefer Factory Method when you want open extension via inheritance rather than modification of a central factory. Module 3 › Chapter 2.2 › Factory Method vs Simple Factory
Simple Factory
A centralized static creation method that returns concrete instances based on parameters. Useful for small-scale cases but requires edits for new product types.
When to use
Small utilities, scripts, or when product types are fixed and unlikely to change.
Factory Method
Relies on Creator subclasses to override a factory method and return Concrete Products, enabling extension without modifying existing creator code.
When to use
Frameworks, libraries, or systems where clients should remain unchanged while new products are added by extending creators.
Misconception
Simple Factory is not a GoF pattern and does not provide the same extensibility guarantees as Factory Method.
Decision quick-check
If new product types must be added without changing the factory code, prefer Factory Method.
Key Takeaway

Choose the pattern based on expected extension: centralized static creation for stable sets, Factory Method for extensible hierarchies.

screens.title: Benefits and Drawbacks
screens.narratorSegment: The Factory Method yields important benefits: loose coupling, improved extensibility, and easier testing because clients depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes. When you need plugins or framework extensibility, the pattern makes it straightforward to add new product types via new subclasses. However, there is a cost: more classes and greater indirection. If your domain has only a single product variant and no realistic plans for more, the extra complexity can reduce readability and increase maintenance overhead. Another drawback is a poorly designed Product contract. If Product does not capture the shared behavior required by the Creator, polymorphism fails and your Creator cannot operate uniformly across products. A practical guideline is to weigh the expected frequency of new product types and the risk of change in the creation logic. If both are high, Factory Method is appropriate. If both are low, prefer simpler designs. A misconception to avoid is thinking Factory Method always improves testability; it helps only when you design Creator and Product with testing in mind and allow injection of test doubles. fullNarratorScript:
In real applications you'll often see classes that directly instantiate other classes with the new keyword. That works at first, but it couples a client to concrete types and forces changes when new product types appear. The Factory Method pattern offers a lighter-weight way to fix that: a Creator declares a factory method that returns a Product, and subclasses override that method to return specific Concrete Products. Practically, your core logic works only with the Product interface and a Creator contract; concrete types are injected by subclassing a Creator. For example, a notification service can accept a NotificationCreator and call its NotifyUser method, never needing to know whether the underlying product is an email, an SMS, or a push message. This makes the system open for extension — you add a new Concrete Product and Concrete Creator — and closed for modification — you do not change the existing Creator or client code. Watch for over-engineering: if you truly never expect more than one product type, the added indirection can be unnecessary. As you explore the lessons ahead, notice the roles Product, Concrete Product, Creator, and Concrete Creator, and think about which classes in your codebase might benefit from delegating object creation.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why direct 'new' calls create tight coupling and how the Factory Method pattern resolves that by delegating object creation. You will identify the four roles: Product, Concrete Product, Creator, and Concrete Creator, and describe the responsibilities of each role. You will implement the pattern in C# by defining a Product interface, concrete product classes, an abstract Creator with a factory method, and concrete creators that override it. Finally, you will analyze when the pattern is a good fit and recognize common pitfalls like confusing it with a simple factory or over-engineering when only one product exists. For example, you'll refactor a simple ConsoleLogger into a LoggerCreator and a ConsoleLoggerCreator so the application can accept future file or database loggers without modifying the application class. These competencies prepare you to design extensible code that follows the Open/Closed Principle and reduces maintenance friction in growing systems.

In addition to understanding the pattern, you will practice refactoring a simple logger scenario and complete assessment questions that test recognition of pattern roles and correct usage. The hands-on activity asks you to define an ILogger interface, make ConsoleLogger implement it, create a LoggerCreator abstract class with an abstract CreateLogger method and a PerformLogging helper, then implement a ConsoleLoggerCreator and update the Application to accept a LoggerCreator. Running the refactored program should still produce the same console output but now allow adding file or database loggers without changing Application. The assessment includes multiple-choice questions that check whether you can distinguish Factory Method from Simple Factory and identify Concrete Creators in code snippets. Practicing the refactor reinforces the advantages: decoupling, easier extension, and adherence to the Open/Closed Principle. Also practice spotting the common mistake: adding a static factory that requires modification for each new product. That contrast sharpens your judgment about when the Factory Method is the right choice.

Directly calling new to create objects is common, but it tightly couples the client to concrete classes. That coupling means every time you add a new product variant you may need to change the client code. For example, imagine a reporting module that creates PdfReport, ExcelReport, and CsvReport directly. Adding WordReport forces editing the reporting module, which breaks the Open/Closed Principle. This problem is not just theoretical: tight coupling increases test fragility, makes mocking harder, and centralizes knowledge about concrete types in many places. A common misconception is that using a single central static factory solves the issue. A simple static factory centralizes creation but still requires modification each time a new product type is added; it shifts, rather than eliminates, the place where changes occur. The Factory Method uses inheritance and polymorphism instead. It declares a factory method in a Creator that returns an abstract Product; Concrete Creators override it to return specific Concrete Products. That way, the client depends only on the Creator interface and Product contract and stays unchanged when new variants are introduced. Consider asking: which classes in your codebase currently know about concrete types and would benefit from delegating creation?

The Factory Method pattern defines a factory method in a Creator, which returns an object typed as Product. The Creator may implement business logic that uses the Product, but it defers the exact instantiation to Concrete Creators. This is different from simply using new: the Creator only relies on the Product contract and the factory method's promise. Concretely, the four roles are Product, Concrete Product, Creator, and Concrete Creator. Product is an interface or abstract class declaring the operations available to clients. Concrete Products implement that interface. Creator is an abstract class or interface that declares an abstract factory method returning a Product; it can also include methods that use the Product. Concrete Creators inherit from Creator and override the factory method to return a specific Concrete Product. A useful mental model is a shop that knows how to process orders but relies on specialized machines to produce items. That separation keeps the shop code stable when new machine types arrive. A common mistake is letting Concrete Products diverge so much that the Product contract no longer supports the Creator's logic; when that happens, the pattern is misapplied and the hierarchy needs redesign.

Let's look at the Product and Concrete Product implementation in C#. The Product is an interface called INotification that declares a Send method. Concrete Products implement that interface: EmailNotification, SmsNotification, and PushNotification. Each one provides the actual sending behavior, but the client will only see the INotification contract. This separation allows code to call Send without caring about transport details. For example, EmailNotification writes a message to the console indicating an email was sent; SmsNotification and PushNotification do similarly for their transports. A common misconception is to design overly broad interfaces that include operations not supported by all concrete types. Keep INotification focused on the minimal contract required by clients that will use it. In the sample code below, each concrete class returns a string acknowledging delivery. That return value shows how concrete implementations may provide behavior-specific details while remaining compatible with the Product interface. As you read the code, think about testability: you can mock INotification in unit tests, isolating client logic from the actual send implementations. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Creator is an abstract class or interface that declares the factory method returning a Product. It can also contain business logic that uses the returned Product. In our C# example we have an abstract NotificationCreator with an abstract CreateNotification method. NotificationCreator includes a NotifyUser method that calls CreateNotification and then uses INotification. Send to perform work. The key idea is that the Creator defines the workflow while delegating the concrete instantiation to subclasses. This lets the main algorithm remain unchanged while the concrete parts vary. A misconception is thinking the factory method must be public and static. It is typically an instance method you override in subclasses. Another important detail: the Creator may provide default implementations that rely on the factory method, so subclasses need only supply the specific concrete type. Designing Creator methods around the smallest Product contract helps keep the Creator implementation stable as new products are added. Concrete Creators override the factory method to return concrete products. In our example, classes like EmailNotificationCreator, SmsNotificationCreator, and PushNotificationCreator inherit from NotificationCreator and return the corresponding INotification implementation. The client — for instance a NotificationService — works only with the NotificationCreator contract and calls NotifyUser. It never instantiates concrete notifications directly. This decoupling means adding a new notification type requires only a new Concrete Product and Concrete Creator; the NotificationService code remains unchanged. A concrete example: NotificationService. ProcessNotification accepts a NotificationCreator, recipient, and message, calls creator. NotifyUser, and logs the returned string. In many architectures the Concrete Creator is injected or selected by configuration; the client still works through the Creator interface. This approach improves testability because tests can pass a stub Creator that returns a test double Product, isolating client behavior from concrete sending logic. These three compact concepts capture the chapter. First, Factory Method is a creational pattern that provides an interface for creating objects in a superclass and lets subclasses determine the concrete types. Second, Product and Concrete Product: Product is the shared interface or abstract class that concrete implementations follow so clients can operate polymorphically. Third, Creator and Concrete Creator: Creator declares the factory method and uses returned products; Concrete Creators override the factory method to instantiate specific products. Keep in mind the practical trade-offs: the pattern promotes loose coupling and Open/Closed compliance, but increases class count and indirection. Use it when extensibility or framework-style extension points are needed. Ask yourself: can new product types be added by creating new subclasses without changing existing code? If yes, the Factory Method is likely a good fit.

Three quick, actionable reminders: design a focused Product interface that captures only the behavior clients need; implement Concrete Creators to encapsulate product selection, keeping client code unchanged; and choose the pattern when you expect extension, but avoid it when a single product is all you will ever need. When in doubt, prefer simpler code and introduce Factory Method when adding a second or third product type becomes awkward. Finally, always check that Concrete Products implement the Product contract in a way that allows Creator logic to remain polymorphic. These heuristics will help you apply the Factory Method where it delivers real value and avoid unnecessary complexity.
